series.title: Reading Ordinary World
series.deck: Five essays on inherited rank, decisions made for others, care, recognition, and fidelity to oneself.
series.note: Lu Yao, Ordinary World (1986–1988). Based on the Chinese essays and their documented factual corrections.

articles.title: Who calls them ordinary?
articles.deck: Three kinds of steamed bun, a boy waiting in the rain, and a scale he has learned to use on himself.
body: In February or March 1975, on a perfectly ordinary day, fine rain mixed with a few flakes of snow was drifting down to earth.
That is how the novel begins.
Its first scene is a group of secondary-school students collecting their food.
## Europe, Asia, Africa
Meals at Yuanxi County High School come in three grades.

The dishes are graded A, B, and C. Grade A contains potatoes, glass noodles, cabbage, and slices of meat. Grade B has no meat. Grade C is white radish boiled in water: a ladle brings up little more than thin broth.
The staple food also comes in three grades: wheat-flour, maize-flour, and sorghum-flour steamed buns.
The students have nicknames for them. The white wheat buns are “Europe,” the maize buns “Asia,” and the sorghum buns “Africa.”
No teacher invented those names. They are not school regulations.
The students invented them themselves.
Sun Shaoping eats “Africa.”
In the opening scene, he stands in the rain waiting until everyone else has collected their meal and gone. Only then does he retrieve the two dark buns left behind.
It is not that he has nothing to eat. He does not want anyone to see what he eats.
## Who decided the order?
Pause over those three words.
Europe, Asia, Africa. They form an ordering, unmistakably so: someone above, someone in the middle, someone below.
These teenagers attend a county-town school in northern Shaanxi. They have never left the province; most have never seen a European.
Yet they know precisely where those three names stand.

They did not invent the ranking. They learned it from textbooks, broadcasts, and adults’ conversations. An account of “higher” and “lower” has reached this county town and settled on three kinds of bun.
What the novel will confront begins on this first page.
That ordering will assign every one of them a place.
And the novel’s title names that place: ordinary.
## “Ordinary” is a verdict
Consider the word.
“Ordinary” is not merely a description. It is a rank.
It means unimportant, undistinguished, not worth singling out. It is always relative to something else. Without an idea of the extraordinary, the ordinary cannot be established.
Who, then, is extraordinary?

At the school, the parents of children who eat wheat buns. In Shuangshui Village, Party secretary Tian Futang. In Yuanxi County, people employed by the county. Higher still, prefectural Party secretary Tian Fujun. Beyond them: the provincial capital, Beijing, people whose names appear in newspapers.
The ordering rises level by level. Everyone knows which level they occupy.
Shaoping knows. The opening scene is a seventeen-year-old boy refusing to let other people see his place in it.
For that, he waits in the rain.
## He uses the same ruler himself
This matters because it is where Shaoping begins.
He does not start with some lofty understanding.
He wants wholeheartedly to move upward.

He reads, not simply from a love of literature, at least not initially. He borrows How the Steel Was Tempered, The Gadfly, and anything else he can obtain. One very tangible use of those books is that they make him different from other people.

His brief, uncertain closeness to Hao Hongmei begins in the same place. Both eat the lowest-grade dishes and carry dark buns; both know the embarrassment. When she later approaches Gu Yangmin, a cadre’s son in better circumstances, Shaoping is deeply hurt.
The blow is not only romantic. The ranking has rejected him once again.
After secondary school, he returns to farm. He teaches for a while; when the school stops operating, he becomes simply a farmer.
He cannot bear it.
The novel shows him working on the hills, looking at his hands and the land, wondering whether this is to be his whole life. He wants to leave.
He tells his father and elder brother. They object: the household needs his labor, and nothing outside is assured.
He leaves anyway.

In Huangyuan, he seeks day labor at the Dongguan labor market. There is no security. Each morning he waits beside the road for contractors to select workers. Being chosen means work for the day; being passed over means hunger.
He sleeps under other people’s eaves. Carrying stones tears the skin from his back. Blood glues his shirt to his flesh; at night he must soak it with hot water before taking it off.
Why go?
In Shuangshui he is “Sun Yuhou’s second boy.” In Huangyuan, at least he is not that.
## An escape
Let us name this more precisely.
His departure is often read as the beginning of an ambitious young man’s refusal of mediocrity: he goes out to make his way in the world.
More precisely, he is escaping a rank.
Not poverty. In Huangyuan he endures worse deprivation than at home: sleeping under eaves, eating leftovers, doing the heaviest work. What he wants to escape is the place already written for him.
A farmer’s son becoming a farmer is entirely normal within that ordering, even proper. Nobody sees anything wrong with it.
He does.
He cannot explain why. Letters to his sister Lanxiang and conversations with his friend Jin Bo do not settle it. He knows only that he cannot spend his whole life in Shuangshui.

That “cannot” is the first thing in him that, in this reading, is truly his own. Nobody handed it to him. His family opposes it, the village does not understand, and he cannot adequately explain it himself.
It has nothing to do with his usefulness.
Staying to farm would be useful. Going out for day labor, wearing out his body, with no clear future and no money to send home, is a loss on any practical ledger.
Yet he has to go.
## His brother stays
In the same family, someone makes the opposite choice.
Sun Shaoan leaves school at thirteen.
He has qualified for junior secondary school, ranking third in the county. But the family cannot afford it. His father tells him that the household can no longer manage: he cannot continue studying.
Then I will stop, he says.

He becomes a farmer and supports the family from thirteen onward. At the opening of the novel, he is twenty-three and has carried that burden for ten years: supporting his parents, keeping his siblings in school, and managing the household’s work.
Leaving has never been his project.
The brothers are the novel’s two legs: one must go, the other must stay.
What matters here is that neither imperative can be explained simply as an order from outside.

Shaoan does not stay because he lacks the ability to leave. He is the village’s most capable young man and later builds a brickworks known throughout the county. He stays because he judges that the family cannot do without him.
Shaoping does not leave because he has some special resource waiting outside. He has nothing. He leaves because he judges that he cannot remain.
Each decides there is something he must do. Each does it.
Within the ordinary/extraordinary ranking, both acts remain ordinary. A farmer stays in his village; a farmer’s son becomes a casual laborer. Neither warrants notice.
## The novel’s real question
Here is where this essay arrives.
The novel is called Ordinary World.
A familiar reading takes the title to mean that these are ordinary people with extraordinary spirits.
That moving formulation has appeared on book jackets, in readers’ essays, and in quotations for decades.
But it has a problem.
It applies for a promotion on their behalf.
Its logic is that although their social standing is low, they are hardworking, resilient, and idealistic, and therefore are extraordinary after all.
Notice what that does. It does not question the ranking. It tries to move these people one place up.
Yet that ranking is precisely what weighs on them.
The students named the buns themselves. Shaoping waits for everyone to leave because he too accepts the ordering. His later departure is partly an effort to escape his place within it.
If the novel finally means only “they are extraordinary after all,” it has used the same ruler to award them a slightly better score.
What happens in the book is much harder than that.

The next four essays will examine it in turn: a man deciding for someone else; a woman spending all her strength; a woman returning to a man she does not love; a woman dying; a man ultimately choosing to return underground.
The final essay will ask the question already contained in the title:
Is fidelity to oneself ordinary or extraordinary?
First comes Shaoan.
He is among the novel’s most admired people: responsible, enduring, devoted to his family, carrying the burden from thirteen onward.
Yet one of his most consequential acts is a decision made for another person.
Her name is Tian Runye.
Ordinary World, by Lu Yao, published in 1986–1988. The Chinese essay uses the three-volume People’s Literature Publishing House edition.

articles.title: He decided for her
articles.deck: Refusing love is a right. Claiming to know another person’s future is something else.
body: Tian Runye sends word asking Sun Shaoan to come to the county town.
He goes. They meet and walk together for a long time.
Then she says what she has come to say.
Her meaning is clear: she wants to be with him. She does not mind that he is a farmer or what others will say. She can find a way.
Shaoan refuses.
The form of his refusal is one of the novel’s most consequential gestures.
## He does not say he does not love her
First, let us describe the act accurately.
Shaoan does not say he has no feelings for her.
They grew up together. Their childhood closeness is known throughout the village. The novel never leaves his affection for her in doubt.
He says something else.

In substance, he says: Runye is a teacher, employed by the state and entitled to commodity grain; he is a farmer scratching a living from the soil. They are not a suitable match. He cannot hold her back. She will regret it.
Each difficulty he names is real.

The urban–rural divide was material: different household registrations, grain supplies, occupations, and consequences for the registration of future children. A teacher with state grain entitlements marrying a farmer would provoke county-wide comment. Her uncle Tian Fujun is an official; the marriage would involve an entire family.
His arithmetic is not mistaken.
But it is her account he is adding up.
## The account is not his
Here is the central issue.
Rejecting someone’s affection is not itself the problem. That is his right; anyone may refuse a relationship.
What he does here is calculate Runye’s future for her, reach a conclusion, and act on it.
The conclusion is: “She will regret being with me.”
But that conclusion concerns her life.
She has already spoken. She has considered the risks. As a teacher, she knows what registration means and what resistance her family will offer. She has thought, and then come to him.
That afternoon, she offers a decision of her own.
He does not receive it. He withdraws it for her.
The two acts look alike from outside: in either case, he has refused her.
The difference lies in the reason he gives.
“I do not want to be with you” would state his decision. That would be enough.
What he says is: “You will regret it.”
The sentence claims to know her future mind better than she does, and on that ground settles the matter for her.
## Another reason he does not state
Looking further, we find something more concrete.
There is another immediate reason Shaoan cannot marry Runye: he supports a household.

His father is aging, his younger siblings are at school, and the family is desperately poor. Marrying her seems to require going to town, or at least acquiring a position commensurate with hers. To him, that would mean abandoning the household that depends on him.
He understands that burden. But he does not put it to Runye in those terms.
He says: “You will regret it.”
One reason has been substituted for another.
“I cannot leave” concerns his circumstances and his choice. He is entitled to make that choice.
“This is for your good” is the reason he presents instead.
It sounds more honorable and is harder to answer: nobody can prove in advance that they will never regret a decision.
One of the book’s most admired people makes a defining decision in this way.
To be clear, he is not a villain or a schemer.
He probably sincerely believes that life with him would make Runye suffer. He probably believes he is considering her welfare. People often sincerely mean well when deciding for others.
The question is not the sincerity of the motive. It is whose decision this is.
## What follows
Runye is devastated for a long time.
Later she is steered into marrying Li Xiangqian, a driver from a reasonably comfortable official’s family: an unassuming man who genuinely likes her.
She marries him.
For years afterward she does not share his bed. She withdraws into a room, neither quarreling nor seeking divorce.
Xiangqian cannot bear it and begins drinking heavily. After drinking, he crashes his vehicle and loses both legs.
That is the subject of the third essay.
For now, remember that the afternoon’s decision is followed by years like these.
## The woman he marries
After refusing Runye, Shaoan goes to Shanxi.
He meets a prospective bride and settles the marriage within days. She is He Xiulian, from a poor household, attractive and direct.
The match is made possible by one condition: her family does not require a bride price.
For a rural household, marrying a son can be its greatest expense, leaving debts for years. Shaoan’s family cannot pay it.
Xiulian says she does not need it. It is the man she wants.
She follows him to Shuangshui, into a household that cannot even provide a decent cave dwelling for them.
## Spending herself
Xiulian is easy to read past. We should not.
What does she do after arriving?
She works.

She works alongside Shaoan from before dawn until after dark. After they establish a separate household in a dilapidated cave dwelling, she keeps working. When he needs capital for a brickworks, she goes to her own family to borrow it.
The first venture makes money. He expands and hires a supposed technical expert, but the man cannot deliver what he promises. A failed firing ruins the bricks. The business collapses into debt.
It is Shaoan’s darkest period. He hides at home, dreads the creditors who come to the door, and loses his ability to face the world.
Xiulian sustains him.
She does not reproach him. Money is external to life, she tells him; as long as they are still here, they can begin again. She stays near him, insisting that he eat and go outside.
The brickworks eventually starts again and grows.

Shaoan becomes the village’s successful entrepreneur. His household joins those earning over ten thousand yuan a year; he receives county praise and appears in newspapers. He rebuilds the village school.
Around this time, Xiulian begins to cough.
At first it is taken for irritation from brick dust. Then she coughs up blood.
The hospital diagnosis is lung cancer.
## The shape of this life
Put the sequence together.
She enters the household when it has nothing, asking no bride price.
She gives years to the heaviest work, including the smoke, heat, and dust around the brick kilns.
She borrows from her own family and helps carry them through their worst days.
Just as the household finally prospers, she falls ill.
The novel describes Shaoan’s response with restraint. He sits there, unable to speak.
He has worked to improve this family’s life. When that improvement finally arrives, the person who endured its hardest years beside him receives a terminal diagnosis.
The promised ease scarcely reaches her.
## Not merely fate
The easiest reading is that fate has played a cruel trick: goodness receives no reward.
But this essay does not read the sequence simply as fate.
Xiulian has lung cancer. The narrative has also placed her amid years of exhausting labor, including work at the kilns.
Lu Yao supplies no medical analysis establishing a cause. He repeatedly puts work before us: smoke, ash, earth, heat, morning to night.
Reading her illness beside that labor makes the bodily cost of this life visible.
Why such work? The household needs to survive, Shaoan wants to build the business, and the routes visible to her are painfully narrow.
The essay reads this not as a decree from heaven but as an exchange: she spends her body for the household’s chance to rise.
That chance arrives when she can no longer make use of it.
## Did she choose it?
Here is the difficult question.
Xiulian acts willingly.
She chooses the marriage, the work, the borrowing from her family, and the long days beside the kilns. She is not presented as being physically forced into them or constantly protesting them.
But what does “willingly” mean here?
A poor young woman from rural Shanxi, with little schooling, sees marriage as the available way forward. She selects Shaoan from the few possibilities she can see.
Once she enters the household, work dominates the contribution available to her.
She puts all her strength into it because that strength is what she has to offer and what she can exchange for a different life.
I would not reduce her position simply to exploitation. The sharper point here is that she has so little else to put on the table.
The coldness of the situation lies in how closely “I choose this” can coincide with “I see no other way.”
## Something Xiulian wants
We cannot stop there, or we turn her into nothing but a victim.
The novel gives her a small wish, more than once.
She wants a home of her own.

Not the abstraction “family,” but a cave dwelling for the two of them. At first they are crowded in with her in-laws. She presses for a separate household, a controversial demand that creates serious tension between Shaoan and his father.
She persists.
They move into the poor cave dwelling. Later, when the brickworks makes money, they build a new home.
She does not live in it for long.
What is most moving about her is not only how she works. It is the specificity of her desires: a room of her own; Shaoan coming home for supper; new clothes for the children; plans for later.
Do these wishes increase the household’s productive capacity? Not in that ledger’s terms.
A new cave dwelling does not make the brickworks more profitable. The “later” she imagines is cut short.
These wishes are precisely what keep her from being only a pair of working hands.
## Next
Shaoan makes a decision for Runye that afternoon.
She later marries Xiangqian and keeps her distance for years. He drinks, crashes, and loses both legs.
Then she returns.
She goes to the man she did not love, now disabled, cares for him, and later has a child with him.
This is among the novel’s most difficult and disputed episodes.
Some call it an awakening; others, the final wearing down of her will; still others, an easy ending supplied by the author.
The next essay examines it directly.
The reading I propose differs from all three.
Ordinary World, by Lu Yao, published in 1986–1988. The Chinese essay uses the three-volume People’s Literature Publishing House edition.

articles.title: Why Runye went back
articles.deck: Giving, indebtedness, and a return that does not vindicate an imposed marriage.
body: When news of Li Xiangqian’s crash reaches Tian Runye, she is working in the county town.
He has driven after drinking and overturned his vehicle. His life is saved, but not his legs.
Judging by the preceding years, one might expect the news to have little bearing on her life.
They have been married for years and have scarcely spoken.
She does not share his room or meals or return to his family for New Year. Within this marriage, she has withdrawn herself and endured one day after another.
Yet she goes to the hospital.
She stays, cares for him, feeds him, washes him, and wheels him into the sun.
Later they have a child.
## Three familiar readings
Few passages in the novel provoke more disagreement. The question is always the same: what are we looking at?
The first answer is that she finally comes to her senses.

This familiar reading follows the narrative’s affirmative tone: she sees Xiangqian’s goodness, abandons her impractical attachment to Shaoan, and accepts a wife’s responsibilities. It is a story of growth.
The second is that she has been worn down.

This critical reading says the social order has finally domesticated her. She once had a will of her own and resisted for years, but ultimately returns to her assigned place. That is surrender, not growth.
The third is that Lu Yao gives her an easy ending.

Here the crash is an authorial solution to a problem the author cannot otherwise solve. Xiangqian’s disability supplies her reason to return and gives the writer an ending he can deliver. The objection concerns narrative convenience.
All three have something to say. I think they also overlook the same thing.
## What Xiangqian has been doing
To understand the episode, look at him before and after the marriage.
He has liked Runye for a long time, sincerely.

He is not a pampered libertine. He is a driver, awkward and unassuming, from a somewhat better-off family rather than some immensely powerful household. Around her he becomes too nervous to finish a sentence.
What does he do? He asks others to intervene.
His mother pursues the match. Runye’s aunt Xu Aiyun and her aunt’s father, Xu Guoqiang, help press it upon her. Tian Fujun initially does not know the pressure being applied in his name.
Her own willingness is not what directs that process.

That is the starting point. He relies on the most normal, respectable, apparently reliable route available in his surroundings: approaching the elders, rather than allowing Runye’s answer to govern the proposal.

Her aunt advocates the match, while Xu Guoqiang invokes her uncle’s political future. Around her come the familiar arguments: it is a good match, she is of marriageable age, his circumstances are so favorable.
Her future is arranged.
After marriage, Xiangqian tries every way to please her. He buys things, treats her kindly, endures her distance, and waits year after year.
Those gifts are also part of what bears down on her.
Every kindness is counted as another addition to what she owes.

The novel presents her as trapped. Divorce carries formidable social consequences for a teacher and her connected family; accepting the marriage is equally impossible to her, because she loves someone else and never wanted this arrangement.
Between those pressures, she can only hold still.
His kindness makes holding still harder and harder.
An abusive husband could be hated. With a husband everyone calls exceptionally kind, even hatred seems forbidden. She can only remain indebted.
## The drinking
Xiangqian eventually drinks heavily.
In this reading, his immediate grievance is that years of giving have brought no return.
His reasoning is familiar: I have treated you so well, waited so long, done everything, and still you will not look at me.
The decisive element is this:
He treats his own expenditure as a reason she ought to respond.
It is not his private notion. His mother, neighbors, and members of her own family share it: after all he has done for you, what more can you want?
Within that accounting, Runye owes a debt that grows daily.
He drinks, drives, and crashes.
The crash is an accident, but the essay reads the drinking behind it as the collapse of someone under that accumulating account, not as an event without a history.
## What changes after the crash?
Here is the reading I propose.
After losing his legs, Xiangqian appears to Runye, for the first time, no longer as someone making a claim on her.
In the hospital he lies helpless. The familiar routine of buying, pleasing, and accumulating claims through giving has been interrupted.
In this scene, he seems to have nothing left to offer as an installment toward the response he hopes to receive.
That is when Runye returns.
On her first hospital visit she sees someone utterly broken, no longer asking anything of her. She has not encountered him in this way before.
On this reading, she does not return because she has suddenly fallen in love, or simply surrendered to her fate.
Before this moment, she has experienced their relationship as a continual demand, an account she could never repay.
In her changed experience of him, the crash wipes that account clean.
When the account falls away, the person can at last be approached.
## Why read it this way?
Compare the three earlier interpretations.
“She wakes up” supposes that she finally discovers his goodness.
But she has always seen it. The novel does not make her mistake him for an evil man. What she cannot bear is not simply mistreatment, but the obligation attached to all that goodness.
“She is worn down” supposes that she surrenders.
Then why not earlier? She has held out through years of misery, until his drinking ends in a crash. His disability alone does not explain a sudden reversal in someone who has resisted for so long.
“The author takes a shortcut” calls the accident convenient.
It is indeed a designed event. Lu Yao needs something to open the impasse and chooses a crash.
But within this reading it is not arbitrary. It interrupts the specific form of giving that has kept the impasse in place.
Had he made Xiangqian richer, more powerful, or more accomplished, the account would only have grown heavier.
He moves in the opposite direction.
## It is still an ugly situation
This interpretation must not become a defense of everything that happens, as though we had finally reached a consoling resolution.
There is no such resolution.
The thing Runye wanted has not been given to her.
She wanted Shaoan. That possibility ended in the afternoon examined in the second essay, when someone else judged her future for her.
Her subsequent life unfolds after that decision: an arranged marriage, years of deadlock, a man’s drinking and disabling injury, and then sustained care.
She did not freely select that sequence in advance.
Going back is, in this account, the first act along that imposed course she can distinctly make her own. Yet the opening comes through another person’s terrible injury.
That is not a good situation. It is a situation she can finally enter.
Colder still, the care she provides looks entirely respectable to the people around her.
Neighbors praise her, her family relaxes, Xiangqian’s mother is grateful. She has finally become a “good wife.”
An act the essay reads as her own decision appears to outsiders as her eventual submission.
Their praise makes no room for the difference.
## Two women beside one another
Put Runye beside Xiulian.
Xiulian has her strength to offer. She invests it in the household’s rise; the improvement arrives when illness prevents her from enjoying it.
Runye has had a decision disposed of on her behalf. Much of her subsequent life takes shape within that disposition.
Both are called willing.
Xiulian willingly marries, works, and borrows from her family. Runye ultimately says yes to marrying Xiangqian, remains in the marriage, and goes back to care for him.
Yet “willing” does not name one simple, identical condition in these lives.
It says that each chooses among the few possibilities visible to her.
Who has laid out those possibilities?
For Xiulian, the narrow prospects of a poor young woman in rural Shanxi make marriage the visible route ahead.
For Runye, the costs of divorce, the position of a woman teacher, and pressure from an official’s family constrain the alternatives.
They have not made the available cards themselves.
They choose a card from those laid before them, then must live that choice as their own.
## Something each retains
But this essay does not end where that account might lead you to expect.
Xiulian asks for a cave dwelling of her own.
Her usefulness as labor does not require that room. The household’s work allocation has no need to grant it. She wants it because she wants it.
On the day Runye returns, she herself walks into the hospital.
No new command from her uncle sends her there. Xiangqian’s family does not dare demand it. Shaoan does not direct it. She goes herself.
She does not go to secure a reputation for respectability. That reputation is added afterward by other people.
In the ward she encounters a man whom she no longer experiences as buying a response or claiming one from her.
It may be the first moment in this relationship that does not feel like an outstanding account.
## Next
The second essay examined deciding for someone else. This one examined choosing among cards others have laid down.
The next turns to a woman who occupies a different position.
Tian Xiaoxia is Tian Fujun’s daughter. She studies at university, becomes a journalist, and knows a world beyond the village.
Her role here cannot be reduced to “Shaoping’s girlfriend.”
In this essay’s reading, she is the person who refuses to make a classification his definition.
Others encounter an identity first: Sun Yuhou’s second son, a day laborer, a miner, a young man of peasant origin.
She sees something else.
The next essay examines her, and its argument for why Lu Yao makes her die.
Ordinary World, by Lu Yao, published in 1986–1988. The Chinese essay uses the three-volume People’s Literature Publishing House edition.

articles.title: The Only One Who Did Not Classify Him
articles.deck: Books, practical help, a promise beneath a tree, and a woman with a vocation of her own.
body: While Sun Shaoping is working as a day laborer in Huangyuan, Tian Xiaoxia comes to see him.
He is sleeping under other people’s eaves. Carrying stones has torn his back raw; at night he must soak his shirt with hot water to separate it from the flesh.
She finds him.
Her first response is not to tell him to go home or offer to arrange an easier job.
She brings books.
## How does she see him differently?
To understand Xiaoxia’s place in this reading, consider how others see Shaoping.
In Shuangshui, he is “Sun Yuhou’s second boy.”
A farmer’s son, literate, secondary-school educated, briefly a village teacher, reasonably presentable, capable of hard work. A complete file.
At the Dongguan labor market, he is a casual laborer.
A young man waiting beside the road to be chosen: strong, willing, inexpensive. Another complete file.
At Daya Bay Coal Mine, he is a new worker.
Someone who goes underground. This file records occupation, shift, and pay grade.
None of these files contains Shaoping himself.
They record what he can do, what he costs, and where he fits.
No individual malice is required. This is a normal way of becoming known in a society: through one’s position.
Shaoping also accepts it. In Huangyuan, telling people who he is seems useless; at the mine, he conscientiously performs the worker’s role.
Xiaoxia, in the contrast this essay draws, does not let that file determine the person she meets.
## The books she brings
They meet while still at secondary school. She is a cadre’s daughter, widely read and better acquainted with the world; he eats the lowest-grade school meals.
She lends him reading material.
Reference News, novels, newspapers. They discuss international affairs, literature, and things that have no immediate bearing on their daily lives.
Pause over that.
The books offer no immediate solution to his material situation.
They do not buy wheat buns, change his household registration, or secure a job. In a narrowly practical account, reading them is wasted time for a rural boy who could be doing more work.
Those supposedly useless things are what Xiaoxia shares.
Later, when he is nearly exhausted by carrying stone in Huangyuan, she still brings books. They agree to read and exchange their thoughts.
She does not make intellectual conversation something he must postpone until his living conditions improve.
## She helps him, but sees more than a position
A detail easily passed over matters greatly to this portrait.
Xiaoxia’s father is Tian Fujun, a powerful local official who becomes prefectural Party secretary.

She does use her father’s name to help Shaoping gain admission to the mine’s workforce. She does it without telling her father; it is her intervention, not a placement personally arranged by Tian Fujun.
Their relationship therefore includes very practical assistance.
She also says that after a year or two she will ask her father to have him transferred out.
She worries about his circumstances and wants to find him an easier route. She is not someone who never intervenes.
Where, then, does the difference lie?
Not in an absence of practical help.
It lies in seeing more than a man who needs a different position.
Shaoping has convictions of his own, but he also accepts help. Independence cannot mean that he has never benefited from anyone’s connections.
The books and conversations concern things that do not immediately change his job. The assistance she gives does not exhaust the relationship.
The second essay described Shaoan calculating Runye’s future and acting on the result.
Xiaoxia also has more resources than Shaoping, and she uses them. The contrast cannot rest on her never having arranged an opportunity.
The question is whether helping someone becomes authority over their entire future. The books, conversations, and promised meeting let us see a Shaoping whom a better job alone could not define.
## The promise on Guta Mountain
On Guta Mountain in Huangyuan, beneath a wild pear tree, they make a promise.
Two years later, on that day, they will meet there again.
Notice its content.
It settles no practical arrangement.
Not marriage in two years, not his transfer to the city, not a plan for what their circumstances must become.
Simply a meeting beneath the same tree.
By the usual practical calculation, it is a useless promise.
It solves none of the questions of registration, work, family, or the distance between their circumstances.
That is part of its weight.
The practical matters they could discuss offer few easy answers.
This promise says something else: in two years, we will still want to see one another.
## Her death
Xiaoxia dies in a flood.
She is reporting from the front line of the disaster. A young girl is swept away, and she enters the water to save her.
The child survives. Xiaoxia is carried off.
Her body is not found.
The date of their promised meeting is approaching.
Shaoping is at the mine, waiting for that day, until the news reaches him.
He goes to Guta Mountain and stays for a long time beneath the pear tree.
He keeps the appointment.
## Why does the novel make her die?
Readers have fiercely objected to this decision. Accounts of the novel’s reception include pleas that she should not die and reports of the difficulty Lu Yao himself felt in writing it.
Her death can also be read as an expression of a structural impasse, rather than only a technical decision about the plot.
Consider the possibilities if she lives.
They would have to confront their unequal circumstances.
She is a senior official’s daughter and a provincial newspaper journalist; he is a miner of rural origin. The essay tests several imaginable routes for them.

First, Shaoping could gain a more prestigious urban job through her family. Accepting help need not destroy his independence: he has already accepted some. But making advancement the final explanation of every earlier struggle would narrow what his journey means.

Second, Xiaoxia could abandon her career and follow him to the mining community. That would turn their story into another woman’s sacrifice for love, a pattern the novel already explores through Xiulian.
Third, they could continue without resolving the difference. That postpones the question rather than answering it.
In the essay’s deliberately severe account, each of these routes threatens something essential to one or both of them.
That is how it interprets the decision to end her life.
On this reading, the severity is not merely the writer’s. It belongs to a social structure that makes a shared life, without the sacrifice of either person’s direction, so difficult to imagine.
Her death gives narrative form to the difficulty of joining a miner’s life to that of an official’s daughter without sacrificing either person’s direction.
The novel does not state this as a proposition. It speaks through the flood.
## What remains with him?
Here is where the reading arrives.
Shaoping changes after Xiaoxia’s death.
Not in the most predictable direction.
He grieves, but does not cease living. He continues underground, continues working, continues his days.
Nor does “moving on” simply become pursuing a higher position. Later, he refuses opportunities to leave the mine.
What, then, has she left him?
The experience of her regard becomes a ground for his later choices.
Before her, he struggles against his rank. As the first essay argued, part of his desire to leave is a desire to escape the farmer’s place. He reaches upward.
Her way of seeing him makes another possibility knowable: his rank does not determine who he is.
They talk about books and international events without treating their conversation as a benefactor’s uplift of a rural youth.
Their appointment beneath the tree makes no stipulation about social identity.
Within this reading, she represents a relationship in which his position never has to be his definition.
Once someone has been treated that way, they know such treatment is possible.
## Something that must not disappear
We must not make Xiaoxia perfect merely to turn her into a device that illuminates the male protagonist.
She has projects of her own.
She wants to be a journalist who goes to the scene. Entering the flood to save the child is not an act for Shaoping. It follows her own judgment.
The novel shows her reporting, writing, arguing, and confronting superiors over her work. That vocation is hers, not an accessory to his life.
He is not there when she dies and does not know what is happening.
Her leap into the water is not about him.
That independence is part of who she is: someone with an imperative of her own that does not wait upon a lover’s permission.
They recognize each other while each has such a direction.
## Next
Shaoping later suffers an accident at the mine.
He is struck by falling rock while helping a fellow worker. He survives with a deep scar on his face.
Someone comes to him afterward.
Jin Xiu, his closest friend Jin Bo’s younger sister, is a medical student with a promising future.
She tells him of her affection. Crucially, her letter offers to work at his mine’s hospital after graduation, not simply to take him away into a different class position.
Separately, Lanxiang and Wu Zhongping propose a transfer to the provincial capital. Jin Xiu’s offer moves toward his life at the mine; theirs opens a route away.
Shaoping does not accept Jin Xiu’s proposal.
He returns to Daya Bay Coal Mine.
He returns to the community that includes his late mentor Wang Shicai’s household, Huiying and Mingming.
That is where the novel ends.
The last essay examines that ending and the question:
Is fidelity to oneself ordinary or extraordinary?
Ordinary World, by Lu Yao, published in 1986–1988. The Chinese essay uses the three-volume People’s Literature Publishing House edition.

articles.title: Is fidelity to oneself ordinary?
articles.deck: A scarred miner returns. Must that choice be scored as ascent or defeat?
body: There is a scar on Sun Shaoping’s face.
It comes from an underground accident: falling rock strikes him as he helps a fellow worker.
He spends a long time in hospital. The wound heals, leaving his face permanently changed.
In the mirror, he sees someone he barely recognizes.
## Someone comes to him
Jin Xiu enters the story at this point.
She is Jin Bo’s younger sister, someone Shaoping has known since childhood. She is young, intelligent, studying medicine, with a promising future.
She tells him how she feels.
She has long loved him and does not regard the scar as an obstacle. In her letter, she says that after graduation she wants to become a doctor at his mine’s hospital.
Her affection deserves to be taken seriously on its own terms.

It is not the same as a proposal to remove him from mining life. Lanxiang and Wu Zhongping separately suggest a transfer to the provincial capital. That distinction matters: Jin Xiu is willing to move toward his world, while the transfer would offer another route away from it.
Shaoping declines her proposal.
His reply emphasizes her youth and the difference between the life she imagines and the life he knows.
Then he goes back to Daya Bay.
## He returns
What does return mean?
The mine remains his chosen place of work.
He returns as a coal miner, scarred, to the demanding cycle of underground shifts, washing, eating, sleeping, and beginning again.
The household awaiting him belongs to the family of his late mentor.

Wang Shicai taught him the work when he arrived. Later, as Shaoping watches, a steel beam bears down on An Suozi. Wang diverts it toward himself and saves his fellow worker at the cost of his own life.
Wang leaves his wife Huiying and their son Mingming.
Shaoping has continued caring for them. In the final scene, he returns to the mining community.
Huiying, Mingming, and the little dog come toward him.
The novel ends there.
## An ending that disappoints readers
This ending has long been criticized.
After all Shaoping’s effort, reading, encounters with the wider world, and love for Xiaoxia, some readers see only a miner returning with a scar to a widow’s household.
What kind of ending is that?
Some see Lu Yao’s limitation: the protagonist is sent back to land and labor. Others call it failure, an inability to break free from his origins.
Another reading calls it maturity: he has finally accepted being ordinary.
These readings use the same ruler.
They score the ending by asking whether he has moved up or down.
## The ruler from the first essay
Recall the nicknames for the three kinds of steamed bun: Europe, Asia, Africa.
They form a ranking that teenagers invent locally while reproducing distinctions they already know.
That ordering never leaves the novel.
It extends level by level: farmers below workers, state employees above them, officials’ children higher still, the provincial capital and Beijing at the summit.
Characters know their place and one another’s place within it.

Shaoan uses it when he calls himself and Runye an unsuitable match. The proposed marriage to Xiangqian relies on his favorable family circumstances. Shaoping accepts it when he waits in the rain to collect his dark buns unseen.
“Ordinary” is a reading on this ruler.
Not merely a description, but a rank.
To ask whether the final Shaoping is ordinary or extraordinary is already to measure him with it.
On that scale, a scarred miner returning to a widow’s household stands low.
Calling him extraordinary because of his ideals, endurance, and rich inner life merely moves him one notch higher on the same scale.
Both answers accept its authority.
## He puts the ruler down
Here is the judgment toward which these five essays have been moving.
Shaoping’s change is not from ordinary to extraordinary, nor from discontent to resignation.
It is a change in the authority he grants that ruler.
Consider how it happens.
In Shuangshui he measures himself, finds himself low, and wants to leave.
In Huangyuan, under the eaves and beneath loads of stone, he still feels the pressure of not being able to remain what he is.
At the mine, that measure begins to loosen.
At first he is frightened and considers leaving. Gradually he discovers that he is needed underground, useful, and good at the work.
His mentor, fellow workers, and shift leaders recognize him not simply for his schooling or imagined future.
They know him as capable and dependable.
That recognition is not reducible to his inherited position.
Wang Shicai’s rescue of another worker gives Shaoping an especially powerful encounter with what such regard can require.
In that moment a person acts to protect another person from a deadly steel beam. Registration, occupation, origin, and prospects do not calculate whose life is worth saving.
One worker places his own body in danger for another.
## What does he refuse?
Return to Jin Xiu.
Common explanations invoke shame about his disfigurement or continuing fidelity to Xiaoxia.
The essay seeks a broader account, but the facts do not permit those motives simply to be dismissed.
We must first distinguish what is actually offered.
Jin Xiu offers love and a willingness to work at the mine’s hospital. The separate proposal from Lanxiang and Wu Zhongping offers a move to the provincial capital.
The latter can be read as an opportunity to move upward in the social ranking; the former cannot automatically be given the same name.
Shaoping has previously resisted letting better-connected people arrange his direction.
Xiaoxia has helped him obtain work at the mine. Accepting that assistance has not meant handing other people permanent authority over where he must go next.
Jin Xiu’s offer is nevertheless distinct. Treating her love merely as promotion in romantic wrapping would repeat the reduction of a person to a social function.
He declines both this relationship and the proposed transfer, but they need not have identical reasons.
The essay’s claim that he refuses the ruler is strongest when attached to his chosen destination, not when it erases the particularity of the woman he refuses.
Otherwise, his departure from Shuangshui, stone-carrying in Huangyuan, and mining years could all be retrospectively presented as steps whose only purpose was a better rank.
His return resists that single account of what the journey was for.
## What does he want?
Now we can return to the question: is fidelity to oneself ordinary or extraordinary?
The question fails in a specific way.
Ordinary and extraordinary are comparative terms. They require a frame of reference: ordinary beside whom, extraordinary beside whom? They place someone in relation to others.
Fidelity to oneself is not a position in that ranking.
My fidelity does not defeat yours. The two do not form a competition or a hierarchy.
The concepts belong to different coordinates.
A person can occupy the lowest social rank without that rank settling whether their life is their own.
A miner at Daya Bay stands low by the inherited measure.
Yet the essay locates the significance of Shaoping’s life in the judgments he makes there.
He chooses to leave Shuangshui, become a miner, decline routes others propose, and return to the community that includes Wang Shicai’s family.
These are decisions he strives to keep from being made for him.
In the second essay, Shaoan decides Runye’s future for her. In the third, Runye chooses among possibilities laid out under others’ power.
Shaoping’s journey emphasizes his resistance to allowing another person to take that authority.
That is the difference under examination. It is not a higher rank or a better external score.
## What does the title say?
Now look again at the title.
Ordinary World.
The familiar account is of ordinary people leading extraordinary lives in an ordinary world.
The reading developed here proposes something else.
“Ordinary” can describe not the people but the world doing the measuring.
The world scores everyone, sorting people as it sorts the three buns: Europe, Asia, Africa, one level after another.
The ranking itself is ordinary: ubiquitous, unexceptional, available in some form in every period and place.
Beneath it, people do things that cannot be settled by their rank.
Shaoping leaves. Shaoan stays. Xiulian wants her own cave dwelling. Runye enters the hospital room. Xiaoxia enters the flood. Wang Shicai saves a fellow worker.
None of those acts is exhausted by the score that ruler could assign it.
Each is an act made by the particular person.
## Lu Yao
A final word about the author.
Lu Yao completed the novel in 1988 and died in 1992, four years later, aged forty-two.

He lived with serious material difficulties during its making. He stayed in mining areas, including Tongchuan, and went underground with miners. Shaoping’s underground world draws on things he went to see.
In Morning Begins at Noon, he records the working life: cheap cigarettes, strong tea, very long writing days, and declining health.
The novel won the Mao Dun Literature Prize in 1991. A widely repeated account says he had to borrow money from his younger brother to attend the award ceremony.
Another story records a bitter remark after his return, a small part of the anger surrounding the award.
Such stories are often told as the tragic heroism of a writer.
That is not the point I want to make.
A million-character novel, written through years of exhaustion and illness, is hard to justify on a narrowly practical ledger.
He could have chosen not to undertake it. Life had already made him famous; he could have written shorter, lighter, faster books.
Instead, he devoted years to this one. He completed it, and died four years afterward.
Its value cannot be read directly from practical return.
The project was his own.
## In closing
Bring the five essays together.

Students give three buns the names Europe, Asia, and Africa. They did not invent the wider ranking but know its positions exactly. The novel’s people inhabit that ordering and recognize where it places them.
Yet within it, acts occur that its scale cannot adequately measure.

Shaoan calculates Runye’s future with “you will regret it,” although the account is hers. Xiulian puts her strength into a household’s rise and falls ill as prosperity arrives. Runye moves through choices shaped by others until she enters a ward where, in this reading, the demand for repayment has fallen away. Xiaoxia sees Shaoping without making rank his definition, while her leap into the flood belongs to her own life. Wang Shicai dies saving a fellow worker, with Shaoping witnessing what that act means.
Finally, Shaoping returns to the mine with a scar.
The ruler places him low.
These essays argue that it has never adequately measured him.
Fidelity to oneself is neither ordinary nor extraordinary.
It is not on that scale.
The three buns still bear their nicknames. The ranking has not stopped.
Yet a person can inhabit its lowest category and make a life their own.
That is what this reading finds in the novel.
Ordinary World, by Lu Yao, published in 1986–1988 and awarded the Mao Dun Literature Prize in 1991. The Chinese essay uses the three-volume People’s Literature Publishing House edition.
